newsitem.title: UK: Ivory Coast debt deal to be closed by mid-year - BNP.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast debt deal to be closed by mid-year - BNP.

text.p: A plan to restructure $7.2 billion in outstanding commercial debt for the Ivory Coast should result in a set of new Brady-style bonds before the middle of 1997, the chief negotiator of the deal said on Wednesday.

"We anticipate to close and implement the deal and issue the bonds before the end of the second quarter of 1997," said Thierry Desjardins, president of the steering committee charged with renegotiating Ivory Coast's debt for the London club of commercial creditors.
Finance Minister N'Goran Niamien said the deal should allow the Ivory Coast to resume good relations with the international financial community.
"We have every hope that this agreement will be very well understood by the banking creditors and they will give full backing to the restructuring arrangement," he said.
"We hope we can renew a trusting relationship with the whole financial community."
Desjardins, who is senior vice president at Banque Nationale de Paris, said the first significant date was February 11 -- the final trading date for defaulted Ivorian debt.
"It will not be possible to trade existing London club debt after February 11," he said.

"March 4 is the deadline for settlement of all pending assignments and March 12 is the deadline for all creditors who want to participate in the 1997 debt restructuring to send in their commitment letters," he said.
He said the mid-year closure target was an anticipated date, but the other dates were fixed.
Some $4.6 billion of the commercial debt stems from April 1987, when the West African nation ceased payments.
A letter from Niamen to Ivory Coast's creditors, seen by Reuters, said the country was hit by a series of external shocks during the 1980s and a 50 percent deterioriation in its terms of trade.
However conditions have improved since 1995 due to a favourable export performance and an improvement in the level of investment, it added.
Agreed on November 22, the deal's so called "heads of terms" permits the cancellation of at least 30 percent of Ivory Coast's debt at 24 percent of the principal amount via a buy-back arrangement.
The remainder can be restructured into 30-year discount and 20-year front-loaded-interest-rate bonds.
Investors will have to choose which type of bond they prefer. The bonds will be denominated in French francs and dollars. There will also be a 20-year past due interest bond.
Niamien said if the banking creditors opted for the longer maturity bonds, this would be more expensive for the Ivory Coast intitially but would be easier for it to service.
Ivory Coast's ability to meet its payments long term would weigh in the creditors' decisions.
"We have to bring into the analysis this idea of risk, which is why we hope there will be a fifty-fifty split between the two options by the creditors," he said.

The World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and some of the country's bilateral creditors will meet the start-up costs of the deal, which includes the cost of zero-coupon French and U.S. Treasuries to be used as collateral.
The steering committee headed by BNP also includes Credit Lyonnais, Societe Generale, Chase Manhattan and Citibank. SBC Warburg is advising the Ivory Coast through the process.

Niamien said he saw little prospect of Ivory Coast returning to the international capital markets until it ceased to be a International Development Association country -- one which borrows from the World Bank affiliate at concessional rates extended to the world's poorest countries. "Regarding our debt policy, we will be extremely cautious," he said.
